chunks.text: To appear today. A bit of background on Consumer NZ. We're a consumer research and advocacy organization. We've been representing the interests of New Zealand consumers since 1959. Let's cut to the chase. We've been calling for meaningful penalties under the Fair Trading Act for many years. We're really supportive of the fact that the bill increases penalties to the greater of $5 million or three times the commercial gain or loss avoided, or the value of the relevant transaction.

I'll kind of break that down on why we support each of those in a second. We think this is a significant but necessary shift. The purpose of a penalty is not simply to punish a business after the event. It's to deter behavior and the harm from that behavior before it occurs. Penalties need to be high enough that complying with the law is always the rational commercial choice.

If the cost of non-compliance is lower than the benefit gained, then the law becomes part of a business risk calculation, and that's not good enough for consumers, and it's not fair to the many businesses who do do the right thing. For too long, penalties for breaches of the Fair Trading Act have been too low to act as an effective deterrent, particularly for larger businesses. We see the consequences of weak deterrents and the kinds of Fair Trading Act breaches Consumer NZ has repeatedly raised concerns about. Misleading or inaccurate prices, promotions that are

not genuine, hidden or unavoidable fees, greenwashing and other misleading environmental claims, and dodgy claims about products or services that are difficult for consumers to test before they buy. These are not abstract legal problems. They affect household budgets and consumer trust every day. The Fair Trading Act is one of the core pieces of legislation that underpins confidence in markets.

It sets the baseline expectation that businesses must not mislead consumers or engage in unfair conduct. But a baseline only works if the consequences for breaching are meaningful. Repeated breaches in the grocery sector, for example, are ubiquitous, and they're a great example of where the current law is failing to deter misleading conduct in relation to inaccurate shelf pricing or misleading discounting, and where the current maximums are not enough to incentivize the duopoly to modernize these systems.

If they were, cases wouldn't currently be before the courts under the Fair Trading Act. Meaningful Fair Trading Act penalties can help mitigate some of the harm caused by the lack of meaningful competition in that and other sectors in the economy. This matters even more in the current cost of living environment. New Zealanders are watching every dollar.

If the shelf price is wrong, or if a special is not really a saving, if green claims are false, or if unavoidable fees are revealed late in the transaction, consumers are not just inconvenienced, they may pay more than expected, lose confidence in the market, or be forced to spend time and energy trying to resolve a problem they never should have faced.

Similarly, with better deterrence, the Commerce Commission would need to spend less of its investigative and enforcement budget on businesses who should know better and have the capacity to comply, like the supermarkets or the airlines or the banks or the telcos, but see compliance as a cost of doing business.

International platform businesses like Meta or Google likely question whether existing penalties are a joke when they compare them to other jurisdictions. A penalty regime that can take into account commercial gain is therefore important, and we strongly support this aspect of the bill. It helps ensure that businesses cannot profit from misconduct.

It also means penalties can better reflect the size and seriousness of the conduct, rather than being capped at a level that may be significant for small businesses but immaterial for a very large one. We also support the move to a civil liability regime. That should make enforcement more efficient and allow the Commerce Commission to respond more effectively.

It is appropriate that the most serious and deliberate misconduct remains criminal, but for many breaches, a civil regime should provide a more practical and faster route to accountability. Lowering the standard of proof to the balance of probability should also assist in encouraging the Commerce Commission to take more cases. However, increased penalties will only be effective as a deterrent if the commission is seen as a credible threat.

The commission must be appropriately resourced to investigate and bring cases. The courts must have clear powers to impose penalties that both reflect the harm caused and the benefit obtained. And if the safe harbor isn't extended to cover these sort of situations, as I mentioned before, telcos won't be able to block scams at the scale and the speed required.

Because without the ability to rely on these third parties- They're going to have to conduct manual due diligence, which will slow down the disruption efforts. Result of all this will be consumers will lose, scammers will benefit, and the government and this committee would have missed an opportunity to make a meaningful difference because basically the safe harbor would be largely useless. We wouldn't be able to rely on it.

And we do understand that members of this committee have got concerns about legitimate websites being blocked, and we share those concerns, and we've gone to great lengths to explain to lots of officials and various ministers that have passed through that website blocking is a very blunt tool. URLs can be changed, encryption is being used more and more, and mistakes can be made.

But if the government does want telcos to try and block scams, and they've said that they do want us to do that, then the legislation needs to help us in three ways. Firstly, by providing that reliance on those authorized third parties as reasonable grounds. And by using these third-party services, I do want to assure you it's going to be less likely that legitimate sites would be blocked because of the intelligence and expertise that these folks can rely on.

They've got deeper insights than any individual telco would have. These providers also have really good processes to unblock things really quickly when needed. And then if the government also puts in place a process to authorize the third-party providers, which we've suggested, then you've got this additional chain of trust and consistency. The second thing we're asking is to not place the burden of proving something is a scam on telcos if the government is asking us to block something.

If the government wants something to be done, our view is the verification burden and the legal risk shouldn't be on others. And thirdly, we're asking that the third-party specialists providing the trusted flagger services be brought into scope so that they can also act swiftly and with confidence.

So to sum up, this committee has a choice: fast blocking with legal certainty or slow case-by-case checking that would let scammers do their damage first. So that's the overview of our points on scam disruption. As I mentioned, Dave from Spark is here to kind of get into all the details with you, and can go into particular examples if you'd like.
